title: Polycrisis Resilience: Minimizing Human Suffering Over the Long Term
subtitle: How economic convergence, innovation, clean transition, adaptation and institutions can reduce the human consequences of an interconnected world of risks
description: The series' foundational framework: how convergence, innovation, clean transition, adaptation and institutions can reduce human suffering across generations.
abstract: Polycrisis Resilience is a framework developed by Hunter Hughes that seeks to minimize human suffering, preserve human survivability, and improve the long-term conditions of civilization in an increasingly interconnected world of systemic risks. Rather than treating economic development, technological progress, climate adaptation, institutional strength, and environmental sustainability as separate objectives, the framework integrates them into a unified strategy for reducing the human consequences of compounding crises. Central to the framework is the premise that resilience should be measured not merely by a system's ability to withstand shocks, but by its capacity to prevent suffering across generations through reduced vulnerability, lower exposure to hazards, improved living conditions, and enhanced adaptive capacity.

The report proposes seven interconnected pillars of resilience: clean transition, economic convergence, diffusion of innovations, climate and environmental adaptation, human development, conflict prevention and institutional resilience, and long-term survivability. It argues that economic convergence deserves recognition as a form of polycrisis mitigation because development reduces the structural vulnerabilities that allow risks to compound. The framework introduces the concept of cumulative human suffering avoided as a proposed metric for evaluating interventions across domains, while emphasizing distributional impacts, uncertainty, intergenerational effects, and overlap between benefits.

The report further contends that integrated progress across all seven pillars can achieve substantially greater reductions in long-term suffering than isolated advances in individual sectors. While acknowledging uncertainties in measurement and varying levels of evidence across its claims, it provides a practical agenda for governments, researchers, investors, and civil society to evaluate policies through the shared objective of suffering reduction. Ultimately, Polycrisis Resilience offers a human-centered framework for understanding how development, innovation, adaptation, and institutional capacity can work together to reduce both present and future suffering in an increasingly complex and interconnected world.
coreProposition: The objective of resilience is not simply to help societies withstand crises. It is to reduce the amount of human suffering that occurs across generations by preventing risks, reducing exposure, expanding adaptive capacity and improving the conditions under which people live.

keyFindings.title: Suffering is the right unit of account.
keyFindings.text: Resilience defined only as the ability to withstand shocks can be satisfied by systems that protect institutions while people go on suffering. Defining the objective as reduced human suffering keeps attention on outcomes: deaths, disease, hunger, deprivation, displacement and lost opportunity.

keyFindings.title: Risks are connected, and so are the people harmed by them.
keyFindings.text: Environmental pressures, socioeconomic vulnerabilities and destabilizing pressures interact and feed back on one another. The IPCC estimates that 3.3 to 3.6 billion people live in contexts that are highly vulnerable to climate change. Vulnerability, not hazard alone, is what turns an event into suffering.

keyFindings.title: Seven pillars carry the framework:
keyFindings.text: clean transition, economic convergence, diffusion of innovations, climate and environmental adaptation, human development, conflict prevention and institutional resilience, and long-term survivability. Each reduces suffering by preventing risks, reducing exposure, expanding adaptive capacity or improving living conditions.

keyFindings.title: Economic convergence is a form of polycrisis mitigation.
keyFindings.text: Closing gaps in income, infrastructure and services reduces the structural vulnerability that lets crises compound, provided convergence is itself clean and sustainable.

keyFindings.title: The pillars reinforce one another.
keyFindings.text: In a qualitative assessment, economic convergence is the pillar that most strengthens the others and human development is the pillar most strengthened by them. Benefits can also run in reverse as vicious loops.

keyFindings.title: A common metric is needed.
keyFindings.text: The proposed concept of cumulative human suffering avoided counts direct and indirect effects, weights them by distribution, shows uncertainty, and removes double-counting. In a hypothetical example, gross benefits of 156 units fall to 118 after overlap.

keyFindings.title: Integration matters more than any single pillar.
keyFindings.text: In a stylized model to 2100, advancing all pillars together lowers cumulative suffering by about 46% against drift, while advancing only the clean transition and growth lowers it by about 28%.

glossary.definition: The ability of people, communities and institutions to adjust to hazards, take advantage of opportunities and cope with consequences.
A failure in one system that triggers failure in another.
A single underlying cause that produces stress in several systems at once.
Several stresses falling on the same people or places at the same time.
The total reduction in avoidable harm to human life, health, security and opportunity, across people and years, attributable to an intervention compared with a counterfactual.
The narrowing of gaps in living standards, productive capacity, infrastructure and access to services between developed and developing economies.
The presence of people, assets and ecosystems in places where they could be harmed by a hazard.
Action meant to reduce climate risk that increases risk or vulnerability elsewhere or later.
Limits within which humanity can operate safely with respect to nine Earth-system processes, such as climate, biodiversity and freshwater.
A cluster of related crises whose interactions produce effects greater than the sum of the parts.
The effort to minimize human suffering, preserve human survivability and improve long-term conditions in an increasingly interconnected world of systemic risks.
The capacity of a system to absorb disturbance, adapt and recover. In this framework, valued by the human suffering it prevents.
The risk that failure in one part of an interconnected system spreads and causes widespread harm.
The propensity of people or systems to be harmed, shaped by poverty, inequality, governance, infrastructure and exposure.
